rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - three-season field experiment (2018-2019) in a solar greenhouse in Tianjin with four treatments (CIF, CIFS, DIF, DIFS), three replicates, measuring N2O fluxes, N leaching and fruit yield. Q2: Section 3.1/Fig. 1a - annual tomato yield about 147 t/ha for CIF and in tendency about 10% higher for DIFs, straw did not affect yield; Section 3.2/Table 1/Fig. 1d - annual N2O 9.6 (DIF) and 9.9 (DIFS) vs 47.8 (CIF) and 78.5 (CIFS) kg N/ha; Section 3.3/Table 2 - annual NO3 leaching 67 (DIF) and 89 (DIFS) vs 788 (CIF) and 603 (CIFS) kg N/ha; Discussion - drip fertigation with straw reduces N2O by 80% and N leaching by 88% vs conventional. Q4: Section 3.1/Fig. 2c and Section 3.4/Fig. S2 - soil WFPS measured hourly (more stable under DIF, 40-89% fluctuation under CIF), soil mineral N in 0-30 cm measured, and N2O and NO3 leaching shown to correlate positively with WFPS, temperature and soil mineral N; Fig. 5 - plant N uptake 45-48% of input in DIF vs 15-16% in CIF. Q8: Section 4.2 - study does not answer whether applied irrigation and fertilisation rates are optimal, would require modelling and multifactorial experiments; Conclusions - complex multi-factorial experiments could not be realised in this study; Section 4.2 - decline of DON leaching for CIF may be a legacy effect of suction-cup installation creating preferential flow paths. Q9: Fig. 1 (means <U+00B1> SE, N=9), Table 1 and Table 2 (seasonal and annual N2O and leaching with <U+00B1> SE), Fig. 5 error bars.
rows.notes: Q3: N2O by static chambers, leaching by suction cups plus tensiometers, yield by harvest weighing - each outcome measured by a single method, no independent cross-check. Q5/Q6: one site, one soil (calcareous Cambisol), one crop (tomato), plot scale (6.7 x 3.6 m). Q7: authors attribute the effect to frequent low-dose fertigation matched to plant demand and the reduced N rate, and state straw stimulation of N2O occurs only under high soil N availability; these are offered as explanations/attributions rather than explicit requirements, so rated no with doubt. Note the DIF treatment confounds drip with reduced fertiliser rate (41% of CIF), so the drip effect is not isolated from the fertiliser-rate effect.

notes: Full text available; supplementary tables/figures (S1, S2) referenced but not included. Tables partly garbled by extraction but values readable.
